title: The corner, and the hardest fair question you can build
summary: Take the crossfire coach's chair: build eight questions against your own debater's case, run the drill playing the strongest version of the other side, coach for two minutes afterwards, then argue whether empty time is where ideas actually come from.
materials: the case file you and your debater built last week
paper and a pencil for the question bank
a timer or a sand timer for the one-minute drill
a parent free to stand up and be your debater

steps.title: The hostile chair, played on purpose and played well
steps.body:
Last week you took on a debater and built a case file with them. This week you do the thing a coach can do that a debater never can: you attack your own side, on purpose, and you attack it well.

Crossfire is the part of a round where the questions are short, the answers are short, and both people are standing. You have sat in both of its chairs, asking and answering, since last season. Today you sit in neither. You build the questions, you fire them as somebody else, and then you step back out and coach.

The rule of the corner, and it is not optional: a coach's question is fair or it is worthless. A trick question, a question with a hidden second meaning, or a question whose right answer only you know teaches your debater nothing at all except that you enjoyed yourself. The hostile opponent you are playing is a real, thoughtful person who happens to disagree. Play them at their strongest. If you play a fool, your debater practises against a fool, and then meets somebody else.

Three kinds of question worth building, and you want some of each.

The definition question. Take a word your debater has been leaning on without pinning down and ask them what it means. Most cases have one of these and most people cannot see their own.

The example question. Their claim needs a real case to stand on. Ask for it. Then ask whether that case is the usual one or the unusual one.

The turn-it-around question. Take their own principle, the one they are proudest of, and point it at a situation where following it comes out badly. This is the hardest to build and the most useful, and it is also the one that most easily goes unfair, so check it twice before you fire it.

And here is the week's question, which is not a decoration on the end of the hour. When you are in the corner you are not talking. The whole time your debater is speaking, you have nothing to do but watch, and that emptiness is exactly when you see what the argument is actually about. Deserts, car rides, the two minutes before you fall asleep and the corner between speeches are all the same kind of empty. What do you find in empty places?

steps.title: Build the bank, then run the drill
steps.body:
Two parts, and a clock only in the second one.

Part one, ten minutes, alone with the case file you and your debater built last week. Write eight questions. Not four good ones: eight. The first three are the ones anybody would think of, and the seventh is usually where the interesting one lives, so you have to go through the boring middle to reach it.

Three rules for the bank. Every question under fifteen words, because a long question is a speech wearing a question mark. Every question answerable in under thirty seconds. And no question whose right answer only you know, which is the line between hard and unfair.

Part two, the drill itself. Your debater stands. You stand opposite. One minute on the timer, questions fired and answers short, and for that minute you are the opponent and not the coach. Do not go easy. Do not go unfair. If your debater is doing well, ask a harder one; that is what the eighth question was for.

When the minute is up, swap hats in the middle of the room and say out loud that you are the coach again, because the two jobs feel different and the switch should be visible. Two minutes of coaching. Name one question that landed, name one they answered well and say what made the answer work, and name one question they should never have to face again because the case now covers it.

Then mark your own bank. A tick beside every question that made your debater think, a cross beside every one that only made them talk. Count the ticks and write the number at the top of the page. That number measures your questions, not your debater, and this is the only number anywhere in this hour.
checklist: Eight questions were written before the drill started, and every one is under fifteen words
At least one definition question, one example question and one turn-it-around question are in the bank
I played the strongest version of the other side for the full minute, standing, and did not go easy
I said out loud when I stopped being the opponent and became the coach again
The bank is marked, the ticks are counted, and I can say why that number is about my questions

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: One take. First, deliver your two best questions the way you fired them, as the opponent rather than as yourself. Then your closing from the debate on empty time. Then answer this week's question straight to camera: what do you find in empty places, and what is your reason?
